title: Lists, Tuples, Sets, Dicts
goal: You will learn to store, change, search and count data in a list, tuple, set and dict; filter/group a list of dicts like a mini dataset, write comprehensions, and understand which box is fast, when and why.

lessons.title: List — one box, many things
blocks: Until now, one variable held **one value**. But if you need to store the names of GEEP's 50 cable products, will you make 50 variables? No. That is what a **list** is for.
**List** = an **ordered collection** of items. Ordered means items stay in the same order you put them in. Square brackets `[ ]`, with commas between items.
A list is like a train: every coach (item) has a number, and the coaches are joined in a line. You can add a new coach at the back, and you can also take one out from the middle.

cables = ["5 Core", "3 Core", "Fiber", "XLPE"]
print(cables[0])
print(cables[-1])
print(len(cables))
Indexing starts **from 0**. A negative index counts from the back: `-1` = last, `-2` = second last. Why from 0? Because an index means "how far from the start"; the first item is 0 away.
**Slicing** = a piece of a list. `list[start:stop]` — start is included, stop is **not included**.
Look carefully: `nums[1:3]` gave index 1 and 2, not 3. `[::-1]` = the whole list reversed. This trick is asked a lot in IQs.
**Mutable** = it can change. In a string, `s[0] = "x"` gave an error; in a list it works.

cables = ["5 Core", "3 Core", "Fiber"]
cables[1] = "4 Core"
cables.append("PVC")
cables.insert(0, "2 Core")
print(cables)
cables.remove("Fiber")
last = cables.pop()
print(last)
print(cables)

['2 Core', '5 Core', '4 Core', 'Fiber', 'PVC']
PVC
['2 Core', '5 Core', '4 Core']
`extend([..])` = many items at the end, one by one
`remove(x)` = remove the first match by value
`pop()` / `pop(i)` = remove by index and give the item back

a = [1, 2]
a.append([3, 4])
print(a)
b = [1, 2]
b.extend([3, 4])
print(b)
Common mistake (IQ trap): `append([3, 4])` turns the whole list into **one item**. To add them separately, use `extend`.

nums = [5, 1, 4, 1]
print(nums.count(1), nums.index(4), 4 in nums)
new = sorted(nums)
print(new, nums)
x = nums.sort()
print(x, nums)
Common mistake: if you write `x = nums.sort()`, `x` will be **None**. `.sort()` changes the original list itself and returns nothing. If you want a new list, use `sorted(nums)`.

prices = [100, 250, 400]
for i, p in enumerate(prices):
    print(i, p)
print("Total:", sum(prices))

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a
b.append(4)
print(a)
c = a.copy()
c.append(99)
print(a, c)

blocks.title: b = a is not a copy

blocks: `b = a` does not make a new box; it only gives **the same list a second name** (like two addresses for one house). A real copy: `a.copy()`, `a[:]` or `list(a)`.

lessons.title: Tuple and Set — fixed data and unique data
blocks: **Tuple** = an ordered collection like a list, but **immutable** — once made, it cannot change. Round brackets `( )`.
Tuple = a final printed marksheet. You can read it, but you cannot change the marks. List = a rough page written in pencil.

10
Error: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment

**Why do we need it?** Data that should never change (GPS coordinates, an RGB color, one row of a database, config) goes in a tuple. Then it can't change by mistake. A tuple is also a bit **faster** and uses less memory, and it can be a **dict key** (a list cannot).
Common mistake: to make a tuple with one item, the **comma is required**: `(5,)`. Just `(5)` is simply the number 5.
**Unpacking** = putting a tuple's values straight into separate variables. You will see this everywhere in Python, in ML code too (`X_train, X_test = ...`).

point = (10, 20)
x, y = point
print(x, y)
a, b = 1, 2
a, b = b, a
print(a, b)

def min_max(nums):
    return min(nums), max(nums)

low, high = min_max([4, 9, 2])
print(low, high)
When a function does `return a, b`, it actually returns a **tuple**, and we unpack it. The swap `a, b = b, a` is also just tuple unpacking.
**Set** = a collection of **unique** items only, with **no order**. Curly brackets `{ }`. Duplicates are removed automatically.

codes = [101, 102, 101, 103, 102]
unique = set(codes)
print(unique)
print(len(unique))
unique.add(104)
unique.discard(101)
print(sorted(unique))
Set maths — questions like "which customers ordered in both months?" in one line:
Look carefully: I printed the set after `sorted()`. A set's order is not fixed, so a set of text can print in a different order each time.
Common mistake: `x = {}` is **not an empty set**, it is an empty **dict**. Empty set: `set()`. And a set has no index: `s[0]` will give an error.
**Where (in ML):** getting the unique categories of a column (`set(cities)`), removing duplicate rows, finding common IDs in two datasets, building a vocabulary (unique words).

lessons.title: Dictionary — find a value by name
blocks: In a list you search by index: `cables[47]`. But how will you remember what is at 47? In a **dictionary** you search by **name (key)**.
A phone's contact list: search "Anna" and you get the number. You don't need to remember that Anna is contact number 47. Or GEEP's item code: say the code and you get the full cable details.
**Dictionary (dict)** = a collection of `key: value` pairs. Keys are **unique**. From Python 3.7+, a dict remembers insertion order.

cable = {
    "name": "5 Core Cable",
    "size": "16 sqmm",
    "price": 4500,
    "in_stock": True
}
print(cable["name"])
print(cable["price"])
print(len(cable))
**CRUD** = Create, Read, Update, Delete. In a dict, each of the four is one line:

user = {"name": "Akash", "age": 25, "city": "Bhiwadi"}
user["email"] = "a@x.com"   # new key = add
user["age"] = 26            # existing key = update
del user["city"]            # delete
removed = user.pop("email")
print(user)
print(removed)
If you ask for a key that doesn't exist using `[ ]`, you get a **KeyError** and the program crashes. The safe way is `.get()`:

user = {"name": "Akash"}
print(user.get("phone"))
print(user.get("phone", "N/A"))
print("name" in user, "phone" in user)
In real code, where a key may or may not be there (like JSON from an API), use `.get(key, default)`. `in` checks only **keys**, not values.

name
price
stock
name: 5 Core
price: 4500
stock: 12
['5 Core', 4500, 12]
`.keys()` = only keys, `.values()` = only values, `.items()` = both, as (key, value) tuples.
**The most famous IQ question: counting.** "How many times did each word appear?" — this is the first step in NLP and ML (word frequency).

from collections import Counter
c = Counter("cable pass cable fail cable pass".split())
print(c.most_common(2))
Common mistake: a dict key **cannot be mutable**. `{[1, 2]: "x"}` gives a TypeError (unhashable type: list). Use str, int or tuple for keys.

lessons.title: Nested data and comprehensions — a mini dataset
blocks: Real-world data (API, database, CSV) often comes as a **list of dicts**. Each dict = one **row**, each key = one **column**. This is a mini dataset — later, a Pandas DataFrame is thought of the same way.
Look carefully: `leads[0]` = the first row (a dict), then `["name"]` = that row's column. Read from the outside in.
**Group by** — the total amount for each city. Pandas' `groupby` does the same thing inside:

leads = [
    {"name": "Rahul", "city": "Delhi", "amount": 50000},
    {"name": "Neha", "city": "Jaipur", "amount": 20000},
    {"name": "Amit", "city": "Delhi", "amount": 35000},
]
total_by_city = {}
for lead in leads:
    city = lead["city"]
    total_by_city[city] = total_by_city.get(city, 0) + lead["amount"]
print(total_by_city)
biggest = max(leads, key=lambda l: l["amount"])
print(biggest["name"])
by_amount = sorted(leads, key=lambda l: l["amount"], reverse=True)
print([l["name"] for l in by_amount])
`key=lambda l: l["amount"]` means: "compare each row by its amount". `lambda` is a small function without a name (remember Stage 3).
**List comprehension** = writing a loop + append in one line. Read it like this: "**do this**, **for each x** in the list, **if** the condition is true".

squares = []
for x in range(5):
    squares.append(x * x)
print(squares)

squares = [x * x for x in range(5)]
print(squares)
evens = [x for x in range(10) if x % 2 == 0]
print(evens)
labels = ["PASS" if v >= 500 else "FAIL" for v in [520, 480, 610]]
print(labels)
There are also **dict comprehensions** and **set comprehensions**:
**Connection to ML:** a model needs numbers. Pulling one column out of a list of dicts, or building a list of features — it is all done with comprehensions:

rows = [
    {"size": 16, "cores": 5, "price": 4500},
    {"size": 10, "cores": 3, "price": 2600},
]
X = [[r["size"], r["cores"]] for r in rows]
y = [r["price"] for r in rows]
print(X)
print(y)
Common mistake: don't write very long comprehensions with three `for`s. If it gets hard to read, a normal `for` loop is better. We write code for humans too.

lessons.title: Choose the right box + understanding Big-O
blocks: The difference between all four boxes in one table (from the book):

blocks.title: List vs Tuple vs Set vs Dict
head: Order
Duplicate
Change

blocks: You need a line of items, order matters → **List**
You need to search by name/ID → **Dict**
You need to remove duplicates, or a fast 'is it there or not' check → **Set**
The data must stay fixed, or you need a dict key → **Tuple**
Now a deeper point that is asked in IQs: **why is searching a list slow, and why is a set/dict fast?**

List = a shop without a register. "Do you have 5 Core cable?" — the shopkeeper checks every shelf one by one. With 10 lakh items, that's 10 lakh shelves. Set/Dict = a shop with a register: look up the code, get the shelf number directly, answer in one second.

**Big-O** tells you how much the work grows as the data grows. In a list, `x in list` = **O(n)** (n items means up to n checks). In a set/dict, `x in set` = **O(1)** on average (constant), because they use **hashing**: the key is turned into a number (hash) that points straight to its place.
In the chart above, the points = list (a straight line going up, O(n)); the flat line = set/dict (O(1)).
The same value always has the same hash, so a set/dict goes straight to that place. That is why a **key must be immutable** — if it changes, the hash changes and the dict can no longer find it.

import time
big_list = list(range(1_000_000))
big_set = set(big_list)
t = time.perf_counter(); _ = 999_999 in big_list; t_list = time.perf_counter() - t
t = time.perf_counter(); _ = 999_999 in big_set; t_set = time.perf_counter() - t
print(f"list: {t_list:.6f}s, set: {t_set:.6f}s")
Run this and the list time will be **thousands of times more** than the set time (the exact number is different on every machine, so the output is not written here).
Real tip: if you keep writing `if x in badi_list` inside a loop, first make `badi_set = set(badi_list)`. The code becomes fast right away. Mentioning this optimization in an IQ really impresses.

blocked = ["u7", "u9", "u3"]
users = ["u1", "u3", "u5", "u9"]
blocked_set = set(blocked)
allowed = [u for u in users if u not in blocked_set]
print(allowed)

Common mistake: assuming a set has an order. If you need order, keep a list or use `sorted(set)`. And `list(set(nums))` will remove duplicates, but the order may get mixed up; to keep the order, use `list(dict.fromkeys(nums))`.

teach.say: Imagine you need to store 50 cable names. 50 variables? No. Make one list — a train where every coach is one item.
Index starts at zero. Minus one means the last one. And in slicing, the stop index is not included.
A list can change: append adds at the end, pop takes from the end. But careful: b = a is not a copy, it is a second name for the same list.
teach.code:
b = a        # same list
c = a.copy() # real copy

teach.say: A tuple is like a list but written in ink — you can't change it. It's for fixed data, and very useful in unpacking.
A set keeps only unique things. Duplicates vanish on their own. And to get what's common, use the and sign.
A dictionary has no index; we search by name. Say the key, get the value. Just like a phone contact.
Remember the counting pattern: give the count so far, zero if it's not there, then plus one. It definitely comes up in IQs.
Real data is a list of dicts: each dict is a row, each key is a column. This is your first mini dataset.
A comprehension means loop and append in one line: do this, for each x, if the condition is true.
teach.code: [x * x for x in nums if x > 0]

teach.say: Last point: searching a list is checking shelf by shelf, O(n). A set and a dict are like a register, straight to the spot, O(1). If you search a big list again and again, make a set.

quiz.why: Start index 1 is included, stop index 3 is not: index 1 and 2 = [20, 30].

quiz.q: What is the output of `a = [1, 2]; b = a; b.append(3); print(a)`?
quiz.why: `b = a` does not make a copy; both point to the same list, so a changed too.
`.sort()` changes the list in place and returns None. For a new list, use `sorted()`.

quiz.q: How do you make a tuple with one item?
quiz.why: The comma makes the tuple; `(5)` is just the number 5.
Empty curly brackets = dict. For an empty set, use `set()`.
`&` is intersection: the items common to both.

quiz.q: How do you safely read a key that may be missing from a dict?
quiz.why: If the key is missing, `.get()` gives None or the given default instead of an error.

quiz.q: Which of these **cannot** be a dict key?
quiz.why: A list is mutable, so it is unhashable; a dict key must be immutable (hashable).

quiz.q: What is the result of `[x * 2 for x in range(4) if x % 2 == 1]`?
You need to check again and again whether an ID is among 10 lakh IDs. What is fastest?
quiz.why: A set uses hashing: a membership check is O(1) on average, O(n) in a list.

iq.q: What is the difference between a list and a tuple? When would you use which?
iq.a: A list is mutable (you can change it), a tuple is immutable. A tuple is a bit faster and uses less memory, and because it is hashable it can be a dict key or a set item. Changing data goes in a list (a list of products), fixed data goes in a tuple (coordinates, a DB row, multiple return values from a function).

iq.q: What is the lookup time complexity of a Python list, set and dict, and why?
iq.a: `x in list` is O(n) because each item is checked one by one. A set and a dict are built on a hash table, so `x in set` and `d[key]` are O(1) on average: the key's hash points straight to its place. The worst case (many collisions) can be O(n), but in practice it is rare.

iq.q: What is the difference between append and extend?
iq.a: `append(x)` adds x at the end as a single item, even if x is a list: `[1,2].append([3,4])` → `[1, 2, [3, 4]]`. `extend(iterable)` adds each item separately → `[1, 2, 3, 4]`.

`list.sort()` sorts the original list in place and returns None; it works only on lists. `sorted(iterable)` returns a new sorted list, the original stays the same, and it works on any iterable (tuple, set, dict keys). Both take `key=` and `reverse=`.

iq.q: What are shallow copy and deep copy?
iq.a: `b = a` is not a copy at all, it is a new name for the same object. `a.copy()` or `a[:]` is a shallow copy: the outer list is new, but the nested lists inside are the same objects. `copy.deepcopy(a)` makes everything new, all the way inside. For nested data (a list of lists/dicts) you need deepcopy so the original doesn't change.

iq.q: Why can't a dict key be mutable?
iq.a: A dict computes the key's hash to decide where the value goes. If the key changes, the hash changes and the dict can't find it. So a key must be hashable (immutable): str, int, float, tuple (if everything inside is immutable too). Using a list or dict as a key gives `TypeError: unhashable type`.

iq.q: How do you remove duplicates from a list while keeping the order?
iq.a: If order doesn't matter: `list(set(nums))`. To keep the order: `list(dict.fromkeys(nums))`, because a dict remembers insertion order and its keys are unique. Or by running a loop with a `seen` set.

iq.q: How do you find the frequency of each character/word in a string?
iq.a: With a dict: `for w in words: count[w] = count.get(w, 0) + 1`. Or `collections.Counter(words)`, which also gives `most_common(n)`. This is the base for building bag-of-words and a vocabulary in NLP.

iq.q: What is a list comprehension, and when should you not use it?
iq.a: Building a new list in one line with a loop + an optional filter: `[x*x for x in nums if x > 0]`. It is shorter and a bit faster than a normal loop + append. But when the logic is complex, there are more than 2 nested loops, or there are side effects (print, file write), a normal loop is more readable.

iq.q: What is the difference between a generator expression and a list comprehension?
iq.a: `[x*x for x in nums]` builds the whole list in memory right away. `(x*x for x in nums)` is a generator that makes one value at a time when asked, so it saves memory on big data. Writing `sum(x*x for x in nums)` is common. A generator can be iterated only once.

iq.q: In ML, how do you turn raw data from a list of dicts into features (X) and labels (y)?
iq.a: Each row is a dict, so with comprehensions: `X = [[r["size"], r["cores"]] for r in rows]` and `y = [r["price"] for r in rows]`. X becomes a 2D list (rows x features) that later goes into a NumPy array or a Pandas DataFrame. For missing values, use a default like `r.get("size", 0)`.
